[table] [tr] [td] [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/38553778-All-about-Strategy-Games/] Follow my Curator Page for more Strategy Games! [/url] [/td] [/tr] [/table] Knock on the Coffin Lid is a roguelike deckbuilder. [h1]Story[/h1] Someone revived you and you're alive again. He wants you to kill someone. The story starts pretty boringly tbh. I thought about skipping it altogether and concentrate on the gameplay but a little bit later, it sucked me in. It gets thrilling and has a nice twist. You can also change the story to some extend based on what you do! [h1]Maps[/h1] One run consists of three different maps, one after another, each with unique bosses. While new runs were the same for the most part, the choices you make do matter and change something. Events seemed to be a bit repetitive. 50 different events sound like a lot but you will encounter the same several times when starting a new run. Aside from battles and events, you will have a few other things to discover on the map, like a shop and a camp to rest. [h1]Characters[/h1] This is where the game gets tactical. When playing with the first character, you will feel like playing a new, generic, and not so innovative deckbuilder but once you unlock the second character it gets way more interesting. He adds a lot of strategy and tactics to the game with many new cards and mechanics. [h1]Battles[/h1] The mechanic of playing cards and how much they cost change based on the character you play with. For example, the first character cards cost energy, while the second character cards cost HP or noches. It may sound complicated now but it's pretty self-explanatory. There are attack cards, skill cards, curses, and talent cards. While attack cards damage, talent cards give you a permanent bonus for the duration of the battle, curses are unplayable and plague your deck, and skill cards can be defensive cards. Aside from cards, potions can be played during battles. Some will give you armor, some recover HP, some lower the costs of cards in your hand, etc. There are like a dozen of different potions. Your Armor also changes how battles play out. Based on your equipment, you get some cards, abilities, or attributes during the battle. [h1]Overall progression[/h1] You can unlock two more characters atm and level each of them up each by playing with them. As you play new runs, your character will unlock perks (4 for each character in total) changing up the playstyle a bit. Aside from that, you will unlock upgrades. When starting a new run, you can decide to make upgrades with you (like the first card of each battle costs 0, start with more HP, etc.) based on what you did unlock before or add difficulties to the run like stronger enemies, etc. [h1]The Balance[/h1] While adding these things, you will see a scale going up, down, or balancing out. This looks like it will affect your future run or if there's a requirement on how "easy" you can make it but to my disappointment, nothing happens. You can add as many upgrades as you want without even adding one difficulty. It seems like something is missing here. This doesn't make any sense overall. Why even add a scale when it has no effect other than affecting your high score? A good idea would be to being forced to even out the scale when adding upgrades. This would be a nice addition and something new to the deckbuilder genre. Sadly, they missed that opportunity. Aside from that, the balance is pretty good overall. It heavily changed based on what modifiers you add to the run. [h1]The Good[/h1][list] [*]The overall progression is engaging and offers a lot of new stuff to make future runs worthwhile. It's also a nice idea to add upgrades and difficulties to your run. [*]Characters are completely different and offer new ways to play the game. The second character makes it more tactical and brings new strategies into it. This is where the game shines. [*]Different decisions can change events and encounters within a run as well as the overall story. This feels great once you get into the story! [*]While the story starts boring, it gets interesting and thrilling soon after. [*]The visuals are beautiful and the voice acting is pretty good.[/list] [h1]The Bad[/h1][list] [*]There could be done more about the scale when adding upgrades and difficulties. It seems like some mechanic is missing here. Otherwise, it is nothing more than a nice gimmick and a missed opportunity. To explain further, other roguelike deckbuilder let you unlock something to make the game easier and you will feel good about it because it feels like you achieved something while it doesn't get too easy. In Knock on the Coffin Lid, it doesn't feel good. It feels like cheating because the unlocks are way too powerful without being forced to add some kind of penalty. You won't feel good about it. You will feel like you felt 10 minutes after cheating millions of dollars in the sims. [*]There seems to be no tutorial and some words/effects aren't explained properly. It says adaptive on some cards for example, which says "Includes special options to evolve into a different card" but there seemed to be no way to use this ability and it wasn't explained further. This is just one example of a few that come to mind. [*]You can just start a run and end it immediately to receive EXP and level up. This shouldn't be possible even in an EA game. [*]A new run has always almost the same maps. It's not procedurally generated it seems (Through different decisions can change future encounters in a run!) or there is just too little content to really make a difference. [*]Too few events and enemies. Over 50 events read nice but you'll get some of the same events in your second run already, the same goes for boss fights and enemies overall. [*]I'm missing a variety of cards with special effects or abilities for each character. Especially the first character suffers a lot because of that. He almost just has cards that do X damage or X block. [*]Some Bugs. It happened to times now that I clicked on a symbol, got a black screen, and needed to restart the game.[/list] [h1]Conclusion[/h1] Knock on the Coffin Lid is a nice and fun roguelike deckbuilder. At first, you will feel like playing a generic and boring deckbuilder because the first character is just that - boring and generic. Once you unlock the second character, the game really shines and is innovative enough. It then gets more tactical and this is what makes these games fun. While the overall progression is engaging and the feature to add modifiers to a run is a great idea, it seems to be missing something because right now it just feels like cheating. Other games make you feel good when unlocking something new to make future runs easier but here, you will get way too strong and make it way too easy without adding penalties. Knock on the Coffin Lid is on the right way to become a great deckbuilder. The last few months showed that these devs care. They already changed A LOT to make the game better. It still has a way to go and it has some flaws, but I'm sure it will get better from now on. I definitely recommend the game to everyone into roguelike deckbuilder! [/quote] [b]Video Review[/b] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vbv87hZx80c [h2]Some of the issues are slowly being resolved every single day[/h2] The game is a mix of gameplay that is similar to Slay the Spire and Darkest Dungeon; it has a lot going for it, including the dialog, artstyle, progression, and voice acting; however, the one thing that always stands out is the fact that this has been in development since 2020, and the game still has so many bugs and errors/crashes that make it mostly playable at certain points. This would regard to anyone who has been playing prior to the game being released. If you start a new file, the game should function properly but there are very few features that allow you to skip over all the cutscenes and dialog throughout the re-playing of the entire game... I'm fine with an error here and a crash there, but having the game constantly updated to destroy your prior runs while simultaneously introducing new crashes, softlocks, errors, and so on is just frustrating, especially when the game itself is very linear as in you're forced to play the game a specific route to actually win. It's not truly RNG once you know what is needed because all you have to do is discover the specific way to get the specific boosts to survive the specific fights in order to progress. What is roguelike is the items/cards you build up along the way, but even these are pretty linear kind of forcing you down specific build paths like Elven Evasion or Anti-Burn stacking. You don't really have a choice in the matter. [h2]Conclusion[/h2] In short, the game has a lot going for it, but because it isn't done (?) it's essentially an up and down slope of... It works for a while, then sometimes stops working, then works again especially down specific routes. I despise the linear part of it; it's not exactly the same as playing Slay The Spire and attempting to force a specific build; it's more like you'd rather travel down specific routes to obtain the specific team / gear and cards to automatically win. The problem with this design is that, as an Early Access player, I effectively lost all my progression, even though the file was still there, the game itself would not let me take the optimal paths anymore, because of crashing. Starting over to get new events and dialog changes and having to sit through all the dialog and unlocking all the specific areas to unlock the prerequisite to actually be able to win the game is killing my motivation. I want to continue playing, but seriously, having to play 9 hours of content again farming the events multiple times to get the specifics done throwing awesome builds away, is just demoralizing. I don't wish to post a poor review, but the game's complete release as of August 8th, 2024 is unplayable for old save files since it crashes at specific points and requires a new save file, and there are frequent softlock crashes while reading the book of monsters, items, and so on before starting a new game one those files. It's worth a play so long as this is your first time playing it, if you're returning you have to start from the very beginning. I would recommend waiting a few weeks or months to see if they fix any of those issues unless you're fine with having to restart from the very beginning due to them, but considering the fact these issues have persisted since 2020 up until now... It's a bit hard to say that I see it being on their primary issues and concerns to address.

A Slay-the-Spires-like with very high production value, in art, voice acting, and storytelling. I just finished my first run, technically a victory already. The gameplay is acceptably interesting and engaging, though it borrows enough from StS without changing it that it doesn't feel particularly new or fresh. Though I am recommending this game, I want to add a few caveats. I think the developers did an amazing job with the worldbuilding and the character design. Like seriously, kudos, I'm a huge fan of Medieval and Eldritch Horror vibes, and I think they hit the nail on the head. I think what they missed out on was why/how people play Slay the Spire. I feel like a lot of people play the game as a "hard and fast" game on the side, a quick bite-sized run between other things that ends up spiraling into hours. However, this game, with its heavy storyline and long cutscenes, makes it hard to do that. Sure, you can skip everything, but that takes time as well. It plays slower and takes longer, even on fast mode, which is less satisfying for those who are just looking to play cards and see numbers go up. The tooltips and UI are poorly optimized. As someone who's played StS and a lot of StS-likes, as well as other card games, I can instinctively understand what "Exposed" or "Burn" or "Strength" might mean. Those just starting out, however. will have to read a ton of tool tip menus to try and grasp the keywords, then remember them. It's also hard to get to those tooltips, for some reason; you hover over something, then you hover over something else, but it doesn't always come up. The equipment system, while SUPER cool and absolutely a fresh take on the genre, is hard to interact with. I can't believe I have to remember to equip potions as I go into battle, and the gear itself feels weirdly balanced. Finally, one last qualm.The game itself feels badly optimized. I've got an AMD 6700 and the first time I tried to run this game, I had to shut it down because it wouldn't load. Some of the cutscenes also took a few seconds to load, again cutting me away from the fun, speedy way I like to play these games (and I feel like most people enjoy). Overall, an incredible, pretty, and interesting game with a lot of love and developer time/strength behind it. The flavor and vibes are awesome, and the gameplay is pretty good. I think they unfortunately missed on a major point of what makes these games fun, though, so this one isn't necessarily good for those just looking to enter the genre. I would definitely recommend it to people searching for something deeper and possibly more complex, even if it feel easier at first. 8/11/2024 Edit for grammar and gameplay: I didn't realize that most of the map events would be the same once revealed. This significantly limits replay value for now, though I'm not sure if further steps in the story will change things. The interactions and lore building are certainly cool, but overall, the lack of mystery and unpredictability will eventually make this game stop somewhere. That's not a bad thing, though. Hardcore is a significant and somewhat unpleasant difficulty jump from normal, considering there's an insane difficulty as well. On normal, I was getting to the end without taking any damage, basically. On Hardcore, I can't even get past the first boss most of the time. I feel like this could be better stratified. 8/14/2024 Another edit. Just beat one of the final bosses (judging by the hints people have been dropping, there's ANOTHER). Starting on a new character and the events are all hidden for exploration again. There's a lot of little hints and events that evolve over time too, helping to enhance replayability, even on the same character, not to mention the very different character classes. I still think the balance feels off as of now. Also, to mirror another person's review and my prior opinion, I dang wish that there was an option to skip most story dialogue. When I'm just trying to grind for the deck to beat the boss, I don't really want to bother with reading everything when I know how things will go.

Another Roguelike game where the "hard" part of the game is getting the items you need in the first 3 nodes or you just basically have a pointless run. After the first 3 areas, the HP and damage of the enemies scales in such a way that i honestly dont feel like it was tested outside of the people that made the game. Enemies are able to start hitting you for 73 damage almost right away and the most you can defend for in the beginning of a run is 6-8 damage. Maybe kill them before they can hit you? Nope, EVERY enemy just applies a 20+ shield every round and the most damage you get in the beginning is 8 damage. If your looking for a game where you have to poke an enemy for many rounds and take unavoidable damage, this is the game for you. I wish i could refund this game, its just not fun.

Some parts of this game really rub me the wrong way. I don't mind borrowing a lot of the combat structure, buffs, debuffs etc. from Slay the Spire, but making carbon copies of cards felt like it was done in incredibly bad taste. I felt a similar way about Lies of P (despite loving the game) and other souls-likes. Borrowing concepts and making a game in a similar genre is fine and a certain degree of mimicry is to be expected. The issue is when aspects on the periphery are stolen too. So when I see a card called Disarm, which is exactly the same as StS's Disarm, or a card that resembles Thunderclap in all but name (and copies the thunderbolt art almost exactly despite being called 'Flourish'), it annoys me a lot. Different people will care about this to varying degrees, but on the whole I really like the game so far aside from this. The most charitable interpretation of the decisions made here, is that by borrowing so much from StS, most people will have a foundation of familiarity which allows the game to expand its complexity around an already proven formula. I think it does this really well and I was surprised by how much depth there is outside of the fights. There are plenty of engaging interactions and mechanics and I'm impressed so far.

It is insane what an ambitious and meticulously crafted 'rougelike decbuilder' KotCL is. From even the first minutes this game just blast you with ridiculous amount of production value starting from the excellent voice acting - beautiful hand drawn art and just the banger of a music - KotCL reels you in and the hours just go by while you are playing. The deckbuilder part i would say the standard fare for the genre , multiple playable characters , several classes between them , (insane amount of) cards , items and well the classic of 'you just looking for that perfect combo or build' , you know the usual - but what makes it truly unique and stand out in this genre is the incorporation of the the heavy story and narrative elements , everything has a purpose and a lore , the devs build this wonderful and interesting world around a gameplay elemenet (the element of starting all over again and again) and they just made it work ... and man do they made it work like well oiled machine , every bit of detail no matter how big and small just oozes of high production value and just he general 'care' to make something wonderful and fun to play. Rougelike Deckbuilders are not everyones cup of tea - but in this game case , it should be. - Highly recommended to everyone.

首先，给差评的真的不懂你们有没有玩了游戏，这么丰富的内容和设计，我觉得是超越了杀戮，杀戮尖塔我都没有玩的这么起劲听不下来。 一款有剧情有探索的卡牌，我觉得是神作，未免说我云，下面是我目前自己研究出来的BD，硬核难度打通最后米兰的测试： 凡迪纳斯： 一如既往强度报表，第一次用即可轻松完整通关，其他角色还得配装搞得死去火来， 妹子默认卡牌强度已经足够，感觉她一上来就可以打最高难度的存在。 1，野猪妹，简单粗暴套（第一次玩她，就打爆了，用的这套，太赖了） 装备：精灵全套5件+兽人护符 卡牌：祭祀神灵&重复策略，明知战术， 打法：主打人形态，比较简单，看卡就知道怎么打了，野猪3次机会出来抗一下伤害保住闪避层数。 2，狐狸妹，流血派，依然简单粗暴 装备：精灵4件：脚+面巾+胸甲+刀，宠物面巾，兽人护符（核心），酋长护手（重要，主要用于打米兰人形） 卡牌：快速打击&兽人护符=不断刷力量。强化链接+*2-3+狐狸的撕裂叠加流血（核心，主用于日常战斗）， 诡计+（核心，可以多拿，至少2张，用于快速抽强化链接，以及米兰人形保护核心卡的快速打击） 打法：日常战斗先用凡妹叠链接，差不多时候换狐狸撕裂流血，米兰人形靠不断刷力量，用凡妹打，功能性一下。 3，渡鸦妹，叠火派，稳定但是输出稍慢，强度稍次。（BD还需完善） 装备：精灵4件：脚+护肤+头+刀，轻型头巾，盔甲随意（我选了恶魔甲，但是有待改进），护符用了 每战升级但可以改进 卡牌：火焰主人（核心，带2张，道具复制1-2张，每回合叠火伤），4张默认的A卡全部升级火伤主打， 凤凰+（核心，用来反制米兰人形的吃卡），腐败庇佑&生存意志（用于突发情况保命，然后用凤凰洗回来）。 卡组尽量保持清洁，就上述提到的卡组和默认卡即可。 打法：日常战斗就是上火焰主人后A卡叠火，精灵套叠闪避和回血，很稳。需要注意是打人形米兰， 用凤凰洗回消耗的卡保持卡组完整，如果不幸凤凰被吃，就用女巫之眼拉回来，这一次几乎不会受伤， 所以不用带血瓶，可以带满3个女巫之眼防止凤凰被吃。 比昂： 1，月之德鲁伊，诅咒套4件：剑+头盔+项链+靴子，武器：原始斧头，衣服：随意。 装饰：头颅窜或者腐烂虫螨。 道具：多带蛇之灵药，复制增加精神吸收+或者积极主动+ 卡牌： 精神吸收（回血核心）， 升级尽量多的默认A卡，以及动物速度塞攻击卡（主要输出），暴躁（拿攻击卡）， 沥干果汁或者各种吸血1张（第一图过度）+吞噬（提高生命上限）+， 打法： 从头到尾一直塞狼人诅咒提升精神，配合诅咒套提升力量，人兽状态切换时可以不间断输出多张卡。 缺点是第一个图没拿到回血牌，会死。 帕西瓦尔： 1，老兵，拿机器人，拿找信封的矮人伙伴，献祭矮人。机器人全程陪伴，PS：就算机器人在米兰人形战死了，蛇型的时候也会复活。 2，眼罩（复制第一张打出的牌，一般是翻倍力量，打人拿闪避等），能力护甲（开局多拿2个能力，比如回合+2力量），这两个比较核心 皮盾+小刀（0费格挡和戳击刷减费），勇士之剑（打西德和米兰专用，还能配合刷闪避） 虫螨魔导书（回血+免疫状态牌）。 3，道具：女巫之眼2张以上，取回过载用来翻倍力量，配合眼罩叠力量。 4，卡牌：战斗饥渴+过载是核心，次要核心是献祭和毁灭印记。 其他牌：闪回斩，虚无装甲。 打法：机器人顶着，不断刷高力量，刷闪避保命。记着2个女巫之眼全部留到最后蛇形态。

如果打折可以考虑购入，原价不建议。 截止到本次评论，游戏中个人负面体验来来自于以下几点： 1：汉化不完全/不准确。有些卡牌效果和实际可能有误差，像是狼人角色基础信息里就能存在乱码也是神奇。 2：故事模式容易让人暴躁。在不查攻略和不看剧透的情况下，三个角色只有后两个存在初见就通过最终boss的可能，初始角色几乎不可能第一次就过。[spoiler] 最终boss是强机制怪，且几乎达到初见杀的程度到底是什么人想出来的东西？一路畅通key卡装备都在手，自信满满觉得能一次通过，结果被机制强杀真tm操蛋 [/spoiler]故事模式就是在不断死不断探路开事件优化路线，往好了说这是为了故事性，也体现轮回的感觉，但是实际玩起来确实有点微妙。 3：说是卡牌游戏，实际是集装备游戏。没有核心卡还能撑一撑，没有核心装备痛苦万分。导致难度高一些的时候，为了拿特定装备，一些角色职业要走特定地图路线几乎是出生就既定的。看起来偌大的地图能走的路很多，实际可选择性没多少。 4：除故事模式外，目前其他模式目前只有一个攀升树模式可供游玩。顶着debuff成型后几乎爽不了三场战斗就是结束，还没有开无尽模式能让你继续爽。 如果能接受以上问题，这游戏其他部分基本都算优点，或者说缺陷没那么严重了。需要提醒的是，这游戏大退强退没啥用，日常战斗想重开的话直接菜单选就行。尤其是故事模式最终boss，不要想着后面的那场快死了退一下就是重打这一场，实际退了之后是连着前面的小boss一起重打。不过也有一定好处（或者说bug？）最终boss前更换装备/道具，进入战斗后大退，回到之前小boss的时候，你的装备和道具会变成更换后的，也许能帮你打之前打的更轻松。不过注意，金钱也算道具，笑。

This game is enjoyable, however I can't recommend a game that plagiarizes so heavily. The game obviously "borrows" very heavily from Slay the Spire in many different aspects, which is for the most part okay, however when cards are stolen 1:1 from Slay the Spire, like same cost, same effects, even redrawings of the same artwork! That just goes way beyond the acceptable limits and straight into theft. They also straight up steal relic effects from Slay the Spire and attach them to items you can equip. I contacted MegaCrit, asking if Knock on the Coffin Lid had licensed or otherwise received permission to use their cards, and they did not confirm that to be the case. I believe that there are other cards stolen from other games as well. So anyways, if you are like me, and would not like to support plagiarism, avoid this game, and instead play Slay the Spire, Monster Train, Dicey Dungeon, Loot Rascals, FTL, or any of the many other games in a similar vein that are in the same genre, or scratch the same itch, without egregious theft from indie developers. Support the devs who originally designed what you'll find in this game! And conversely, if you are *not* like me, and you have no issues with theft of other's work, well, Steam probably isn't the platform where you should be acquiring your games.

In short: Nice take on classic Slay the Spire formula. Recommended. It is more narrative focused game than StS, every move is commented and contributes to the plot. It is different for each character. Map is pre-determined but every enemy/event can have different options and outcomes for each character. Story is good and fragmented. You need to play all the characters several times to reveal the whole plot. There are three main characters and each has several unlockable subclasses. Each of those has different playstyles. Unlocking mechanics looked like a drawback for me as it forces you to play a character you do not like. For me it become an advantage as the class I liked the least became my favourite character after a couple of runs. Inventory/card system is a mix between StS and regular RPGs: there are armours, helmets, shields, boots, rings, amulets, weapons, potions that go in their respective slots. Some cards are linked to your equipment. You can buy, sell equip and unequip stuff. The art style is gorgeous. Aestetics-wise it is the best game I've played in a couple of years. Replayability is good. Every character has its own interaction with non-randomized map and variety of possible routes is pretty large. Drops are random so the build is more defined by the run than initial intent, ie this part is just like it is in StS. Overal it is a good game and totally worth a full price.

This is one of the most unexpected and treasured finds I've found this year, and I think quite honestly this is the best of the genre in 2026. I am not a card battler or deck building roguelite person in general. There are a lot of clones out there and attempts to make this genre engaging that fall flat. But this is a Goldilocks game, because everything is just right. Encasing a game in curated pathways that develop in the narrative framework, and ensuring every choice carries weight is a genius move. Yes, we live in the era of RNG and procedurally generated dungeons or landscapes, and it is so refreshing to have a game with a series of open paths that form reliable encounters. Instead of just pure required quests for story progression, you have the opportunity to learn organically what's going on and select the subquest that interests you most. The challenges are excellent and allow you to improve on the starting builds permanently. In essence, this takes the best part of RPG experiences and the dopamine hits of quick rounds to give you a game that is endlessly fun to play and experiment with. I'm old enough to remember when choosing a given build would sometimes lock you out of progression. I'm looking at you Deus Ex. Instead of loyalty to a single build, the variation in cards with equipment tie-ins and set bonuses and predictable amulets that you can pursue make experimenting with your builds part of the fun, instead of a drag. There are many many ways to solve each battle, enough so that the RNG does not screw you over unless you are fundamentally careless or not paying attention. In terms of graphics, the animations are bright and well done, and any minor loading issues are worth the wait. This runs extremely well on my deck, and I strongly recommend the mouse only template to keep your sanity. I have the game loaded up and steam says I've only been playing for 5 hours, when it feels like a hell of a lot longer, in the best way. I learn with every run, and quite honestly guides are not really required unless you want to eliminate as much of the random fun as you desire. In other words, this caters to quite a few different play styles, is pretty much universally accessible, and the only critique of playing on a portable system is the size of the fonts. But since the voice acting of critical cutscenes is performed aloud, it should not detract if you really don't want to read all of the small bullet updates. I find the UI absolutely well programmed and appropriate, with no extraneous information cluttering up the space. The tutorial is, imagine that, an appropriate length and gives as much detail as you really need to start. The classes are unique, and level building doesn't force you to spend too much time agonizing over skill trees, it just grants access, New cards, and starting bonuses. Unlike some other reviewers, I found each of the classes to be fun in their own way. Tldr, this game is really fun. It respects the gamer, and although you could argue that the average run is about an hour and that's longer than some people want from their roguelites, the devs respect you and allow you to exit the game in mid-run. If you're going to lose a battle, you know fairly quickly. If there is an automatic loss button when you are mathematically outclassed, I haven't found it but it may be there. Either way, the disappointment you feel about a run investment is quickly washed away by the rewards both narratively and in terms of experience. Although I routinely recommend games with strengths that are unique or outbalance numerous weaknesses, there really aren't weaknesses here for me. This is well worth full price, and I fully intend on purchasing the DLC. If you've never given this genre of games a shot because you don't think you would like it, I say pick this up over the very famous game that just released a sequel this year that people love, but I found oblique and not very interesting. This game is easily a 10 out of 10 investment. I am very impressed with this development studio and I will be a lifetime fan. Enjoy!

The most contradictory game I've ever played (thus, the review). It is very good and it is very bad. I've been trying to understand why and to like the game for long time. Now I'll try to explain it. The goal of the game creation is clear: make Slay the Spire (STS) again, but with everything much better: art, lore, storyline, replayability, mechanics, characters, equipment, GUI. I was highly attracted by this intent: I've beaten The Heart by all characters, and I really feel STS could be better in many aspects. Everything is promising around here from the first minutes. But after many hours you realize that every aspect ended up bad. Not satisfying, not fun, irritating. No promise is satisfied (except for art). Now, from higher disappointing aspects to lesser. 1. Replayability. It seems replayability was set as key direction for the game design. And it turned out into mania, destructing other aspects. And... it ended up bad, more precisely it is limited by characters and their classes (12 in total) which are really different and mostly interesting. But the main "know-how" idea for replayability is failed. It is: each run player gets more info about points/events on the map (mostly, about drop), so the next run you may choose perfect way to collect best equipment set for your goal / character. The idea doesn't work: - Not all received info is shown on map. Not even close. - Too few points where something important drops. - When you get real goal (via storyline), related points forcedly shown on map, whether you have seen that info before, or not. - Equipment sets exist (and they are fun), but you almost never can collect them: too few shops on map, so you rarely can pass both shop and the point where required part drops. - One character does not see map info got by previous one. So, you have to reopen the same points, which irritates a lot, making the main idea a curse, not bless. - The same equipment differs for different characters; don't try to remember their names. Why "mania"? For example, there is kind of "bestiary": some info about mobs you've met. But you have to repeat battles with that mob to "level up" that article and open more info. Even if you have seen some critical info in a battle, it will not appear there without "level up". So, bestiary becomes useless. Anyway, it is not accessible from battle (as well as story log). When you have beaten the game by a character, the character becomes marked (by visual on its coffin) as "done". Attempt to rerun shows "Do you want to change char's story end?" and clears that mark. So, replayability is planned for losing, not for winning. 2. Clearness. It is not the game where you make deliberated decisions. Did you have cases when you precisely counted all damages and maid perfect turn in STS? Forget about it. First, there will be too much effects on everyone to calculate for sure. First boar on first map will have 5-6 effects. Before he casts more. Second, you never know how exactly the card or your ability will play, how mob will react to your actions, how multiple damage will be resolved. There are descriptions for everything, but they never complete or clear. It is a curse for this game. You will loudly ask your monitor all the time: - Whose "ally"? - What is "severely wounded"? - What is a difference between "a turn" and "the turn" if any? - "While dealing damage" - is it for that card damage, or for the turn? - Who will receive the buff: hero or the pet? - Why the mob cleared of my debuff? - Which buffs and debuffs considered in damage value shown? - What that "sharp question mark" means on the map? (spoiler: possible elite battle) - What is "class item"? (I don't know even now) I can continue this list endlessly. Some info shown nowhere: some cards damage accumulated during battle and you do not know how many; you may have global buffs not shown until you start battle. 3. Deckbuilding and balance. No balance between cards: too many are too weak. Choosing between 3 (reward) usually is "at least 1 working at all". There are clues for some mechanics (synergies) on cards to build your deck around: "Burn" (= Exhaust in STS), "Ferocious", "Piercing damage", "Frostbite", etc. But most of those cards are too weak itself to include them into deck; or those cards can be found too rarely to even try. Except one mechanic: "Bleeding"; it's too strong and you will most probably end up with it. Anyway, shops do not sell cards, so do not worry about deckbuilding, it will never be deliberated. Equipment is much stronger than cards. But cards are played, while equipment gives passive effects, so this makes player activity is less affecting. "Strength" effect (the same as in STS) is overused by heroes and mobs; I don't know if it is author's intent, but it kills all the other gameplay. You never will be competitive if you not count on increasing Strength every turn. Damage values on cards do not matter anymore: who cares 4 or 8 damage if after 20 Strength applied it will be 24 or 28? Mob Strength rising from turn to turn leads to very high chance of getting very high (often lethal) damage suddenly from mobs. To mitigate this, the game has to provide very high "margin" between your and mobs' overall power, so the most part of battles is just swatting mosquitos (even on "hardcore" difficulty). But if you was unlucky to not get that margin, a mosquito is you. Bosses are too strong comparing to mobs, so when you are powerful enough for a boss, fighting regular mobs before is boring. No balance in too many other aspects. Sometimes it seems authors don't even realize how strong or weak something is. For example, one class of 2nd character described: "... suffers less from his curse than others." In fact it receives curse card into the deck (permanently!) ONCE PER TURN. Ok, the curse gained additional positive effect, but it still takes places in the deck. While other classes receive the curse card not even close this often, and one other class do not receive it all. Two close game difficulties are described: - Normal: the enemies will pretend that they want to stop you. - Hardcore: Survive, die, repeat. Nothing in between. I.e. no normal satisfying "~70% run success chance" mode. Actually, real difference is not that high, I'm just pointing authors do not think anything is wrong with those descriptions, i.e. balancing is not priority. 4. Lore and storyline. Ok, the lore is here. Storyline too, no rebukes. But how they are injected into the game is bad. First of all, they do not affect gameplay, just exist in parallel. I honestly tried to read every line of conversations, hoping to get anything useful for my game choices. Nothing, so I started skipping. So sad. Characters just go on and go on, way to much. Voice intonations rarely match text. The lore is about few typical fantasy races, which changed relations after some political changes. A lot of political talks, i.e. tons of referring to places (cities etc.). And... no single label on map. You don't even know where north is (spoiler: at map bottom). Chars literally say "every decision affects everything". In fact, the only place where decisions go: text in final cutscene like "orcs leaved the kingdom". 5. Art. Introductory screens are beautiful, "make it my wallpaper" quality. They make immersion effect. But in battle (where you spend 90+% of your time) the same drawn characters turn into caricature style. Why? All the immersion is lost. Cards art (most important for convenient playing) is totally forgettable and merely distinguishable between cards. No hope to remember card action by a picture. Many card pictures depict... actions with cards. That is breaking the 4th wall at least, but also doesn't allow to remember card action, because, you know, there are not much visual actions with cards exist: they all are thrown by the character with slightly different emotions on face. In cutscenes, mouths do not open when people talk. Arthouse or just creepy?

A spiritual successor to Slay the Spire 1, Knock on the Coffin Lid is more than just gathering strong cards and reaching the end. There is a fleshed out story that incentivizes repeated runs and embraces the idea of resurrection with its scripted events at fixed points that can unfold in various ways depending on your choice, your previous path, and your moral alignment. New knowledge can therefore be used on new runs as you technically go back in time, letting you see how events would've unfolded had you done differently. Maybe you come across an elven archer doing target practice with a live dwarf but misses the apple because your gear stood out and distracted him. The question begs what would happen if the dwarf was still alive? So you go back in the next run and don an unassuming elven armor and see what happens, if it even works, who knows? Gear is also a strong addition to the genre, building your character like an RPG with set bonuses that heavily supports a particular playstyle focus like bleed, tanking, curses, or even gold accumulation. Thought has been put into how fights play, with many new effects but some almost copied from Slay the Spire, nonetheless it keeps the game fresh with interesting enemy tactics to overcome. One negative is that there are too many confirmation prompts, at least let us decide whether to see them or not in settings, most are simply not needed and adds busywork and disrupts the flow of gameplay. With the polish above, this game could easily become one of the best in the genre. Overall a great game.

It's alright. I wouldn't get it at full price. In a lot of ways, it is unquestionably a DIRECT knock-off of Slay the Spire, down to the exact cards and even damage numbers on those cards. Knock on the Coffin takes Slay the Spire and adds an equipment inventory, more varied events and choices, and a pretty decent mystery-vibe. Its art direction can be a bit of a hard sell at times, depending on what you like. The biggest main gameplay difference to StS from the deck-building aspect is that in StS you try to play the strategically optimal cards to minimize the damage you receive. In Knock on the coffin you ultimately want to overwhelm the enemy by building up massive status effects. This can turn battles into accidental slugfests, and keeping an overview of the fight is not easy. In the end, this got to be pretty draining on me, and playing this for more than one run at once wasn't a lot fun.

Knock on the Coffin Lid is a captivating fusion of roguelike deck-building and narrative-driven role-playing that delivers far more than a traditional card battler. Developed and published by RedBoon, the game opens with a striking premise as the protagonist awakens inside a coffin with no memory of how they died. Guided by a mysterious figure, the journey becomes one of revenge, self-discovery, and political intrigue across a fractured fantasy realm. While its card combat immediately appeals to fans of strategic roguelikes, the game's greatest strength lies in how every battle and decision contributes to a larger, evolving story where actions carry lasting consequences. The narrative is one of the title's defining achievements. Rather than simply moving players from encounter to encounter, the game presents a living world filled with rival kingdoms, competing races, and influential leaders whose futures are shaped by the player's choices. Every important decision has the potential to alter alliances, determine the survival of entire factions, and ultimately influence who controls the Northern Gate. The branching storyline encourages multiple playthroughs because different decisions reveal new perspectives, alternate events, and additional endings. Instead of relying on simple good-versus-evil morality, the writing explores complicated political conflicts and personal motivations, making every choice feel meaningful and often morally uncertain. Combat is equally rewarding thanks to its deep deck-building mechanics. Each run revolves around collecting cards, relics, equipment, and powerful upgrades that gradually transform a basic deck into a specialized combat strategy. Victory depends on understanding card synergies, resource management, defensive timing, and adapting to enemy behavior rather than simply acquiring the strongest individual cards. Encounters remain engaging throughout the adventure because opponents introduce distinct mechanics that force players to rethink established tactics. Experimenting with different combinations becomes one of the most satisfying aspects of the experience, especially as new cards and equipment continually expand strategic possibilities. Replayability is another area where Knock on the Coffin Lid excels. Multiple playable heroes, branching story paths, randomized encounters, unlockable content, and numerous deck archetypes ensure that each campaign feels fresh. Even after completing the main storyline once, there are still alternate routes, hidden lore, and different political outcomes waiting to be discovered. Unlike many roguelikes where repeated runs focus almost exclusively on improving gameplay efficiency, this title rewards players with meaningful narrative revelations that deepen the overall experience every time they return. The visual presentation effectively reinforces the game's dark fantasy atmosphere. Character artwork is expressive, monsters are creatively designed, and environments successfully capture the bleak tone of a kingdom plagued by conflict and uncertainty. Combat animations remain clear despite the growing complexity of battles, allowing players to track card effects and status changes without becoming overwhelmed. The soundtrack complements every stage of the adventure with moody orchestral themes and tense battle music, while the overall sound design helps maintain immersion during both exploration and combat. Despite its many strengths, the game does have a few shortcomings. The sheer number of mechanics introduced early can feel overwhelming for newcomers unfamiliar with deck-building roguelikes. Understanding the interactions between cards, equipment, artifacts, and status effects requires patience, and some encounters can become unforgiving if players fail to build an effective strategy. Randomized elements occasionally create difficult situations that are hard to recover from, although experienced players will often appreciate the challenge and the need to adapt. Fortunately, the rewarding progression system and compelling story provide strong motivation to continue learning the game's deeper mechanics. One of the game's most impressive accomplishments is how seamlessly it blends storytelling with gameplay. Narrative decisions are never disconnected from the mechanics, and character progression feels directly tied to the unfolding mystery surrounding the protagonist's fate. Every successful battle contributes to a larger journey of uncovering hidden truths, while every setback reinforces the harsh and unpredictable nature of the world. This balance between strategic gameplay and meaningful storytelling gives the adventure a sense of cohesion that many games in the genre struggle to achieve. Knock on the Coffin Lid stands out as an ambitious and polished roguelike that successfully combines tactical deck-building with an engaging fantasy narrative full of branching choices and political consequences. Its challenging combat, extensive replay value, memorable world-building, and strong emphasis on player agency make it a rewarding experience for those willing to invest time in mastering its systems. Although its complexity may discourage some newcomers, players who enjoy thoughtful strategy games with rich storytelling will find an experience that remains compelling from beginning to end. Rating: 8/10

I really want this game to be good. It's fun a good chunk of the time. But there are a ton of flaws. 1.) There are SO MANY different combinations of events on the map - and sometimes that combination is just "do that 3 more times and then something will happen" - that I know I'm never going to see anywhere close to all of them. 2.) The final boss battle sucks. It's different for the different characters, but on Vanadis it's just a terrible quick-time event that moves VERY slowly, and if you mess it up at the wrong time (about 5 minutes in), it repeats. Mess it up again, it repeats again. You literally can't fail, as far as I can tell. It just wastes your time. If you quit because you have a life or something, you have to repeat the previous fight, which is also slow and annoying. The others' final boss isn't quite that bad, but they're all pretty bad. 2.5.) Also, once you unlock the final fight, it suggests you take pretty specific paths to find the ways to beat that fight, which makes... all the rest of the huge map you have available... kinda not worth it for a long time, if not forever. 3.) Balancing is also poor, as there are some builds that are easy to steamroll (honey badger can kill an enemy just by being summoned sometimes on 2nd hardest difficulty), and other builds that it's hard to get through the first area with or need specific items to be good. 4.) It has a lot of cards that are direct copies of slay the spire cards. Mostly it's its own game, which is why I find this annoying. You made a whole game, with a lot of diverse cards. Why would you plagiarize when you did all that? 5.) The story is mid, mostly because I really don't care about any of the characters. Percival is the only one who seems remotely like a good person, and they're all pretty flat. Percival wants to understand why he was betrayed, Bjorn likes killing but secretly maybe there's more to him, but actually there isn't, and Vanadis wants the throne. That's about all the development they get. Which would be fine, except they throw more story at you constantly, and it's all the same stuff in different situations. If you're jonesing for more hot deckbuilder action and STS, across the obelisk, battle bands and others are played out for you, maybe try it. It's not bad, I'm still having fun with it, it just needs... higher standards, I guess.
